Imran, five, watched Mummy slice a paratha roll in two and stared. His sister Vinita's half looked a little longer. "Not fair!" he wailed, tears coming, pointing to prove it. Mummy handed him the knife. "You cut, Vinita chooses." Imran cut very slowly, one eye shut, and Vinita picked a half without a fuss.

At school, Nilesh opened a shiny tin with a rocket on the lid. Imran's tummy felt tight and hot. He almost said the tin looked boring, then whispered, "I wish I had one like that. Can I have a turn?" Nilesh hugged it close. "I will not share with you. You are not my friend." Imran's chin wobbled. "That makes me sad," he said, and walked to the sand tray. Their teacher had seen it all, and later set a sand timer on the table so both boys got a go.

That evening a small cousin reached for Imran's red truck. "Give it to him right now," said Papa. Imran squeezed the truck against his chest, cheeks burning, cross and muddled. Mummy knelt down. "The truck stays yours and stays special. Which other toy would you like to lend?" Imran thought, then held out his blue bus.

qa.q: Who chose a half of the paratha roll after Imran cut it?
qa.a: Vinita chose a half without a fuss.

qa.q: How did the three sharing troubles in Imran's day differ in what eased them?
qa.a: At home, letting one child cut and the other choose settled the count. At school, saying "I wish I had one like that" and later "That makes me sad" gave Imran words for wanting and hurt, and a timer gave turns. In the evening, being ordered to hand over the truck made him grip it harder, while keeping it special and lending another toy worked.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when Papa told him to give the truck to the cousin right now?
qa.a: He felt cross and muddled. He squeezed the truck against his chest and his cheeks burned.

qa.q: How could the teacher help the boys after Nilesh refused to share the tin?
qa.a: The teacher could keep using the sand timer so each boy gets a turn, and stay near in case Imran feels left out again.

grounding: One child's day shows a sibling's count of halves, wanting a classmate's tin, a friend's refusal and an ordered handover of a favourite toy.

passage:
Ganga, eleven, sat through the ad break with her chin on her knees. Every girl on the screen was pale and thin and glowing, and something in her chest sank. Maybe she was simply not enough.

At school, Samir, a boy in her class, looked at her arms during games and said loudly that she was too dark for the team photo. A few others laughed. Ganga's face went hot, and she said nothing. After class she told Ms Rao, her teacher, who listened without interrupting, said it was not Ganga's fault, and spoke to Samir that same afternoon. Ganga also sat at lunch beside Anand, a classmate who always saved her a spot.

At bedtime Amma stroked her hair. "You are beautiful exactly as you are." Ganga rolled her eyes. "You have to say that." Amma only smiled. "I say it because it is true, and I would say it anyway." The words did not convince her, but they stayed with her like a warm stone in a pocket.

On sports day Ganga ran the last stretch with her lungs burning and crossed the line first. Her legs shook, she laughed out loud, and she squeezed Anand's hand. She felt strong. Then she turned and clapped hard for Tenzin, the shortest boy in class, who came in last with his hands on his knees and a big grin.

qa.q: Who did Ganga tell about Samir's remark after class?
qa.a: Ganga told Ms Rao, her teacher.

qa.q: How did the ad break and Amma's bedtime words pull at Ganga's view of herself in different directions, and what shifted after the race?
qa.a: The screen left her feeling she was not enough, while Amma's steady words stayed with her like a warm stone even though she did not believe them. After the race she felt strong in her own body and could cheer for Tenzin, whose body was different from hers.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when Samir spoke about her skin and the others laughed?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed. Her face went hot and she stayed silent.

qa.q: How did Ms Rao's response help Ganga?
qa.a: Ms Rao listened, said it was not Ganga's fault, and spoke to Samir the same afternoon, so Ganga did not have to carry it alone.

grounding: Screen images, a classmate's mockery, a parent's steady love and pride after a race show four influences on one child's view of her body.

passage:
Dolma spotted a folded hundred-rupee note near the water cooler, and her pulse thumped. Chocolate. A new sticker book. Then Zeenat came up. "Finders keepers! Let's get chips." Anjali stood a step behind, saying nothing. Dolma's stomach twisted. "I'd rather not," she said. "Somebody is probably looking for it." She carried it to the teacher's desk. Later, Anjali murmured, "I didn't want to spend it either," and Zeenat just shrugged, a little sulky.

On Saturday the man at the corner shop counted out her change and pushed forward too many coins. Nobody was watching. Dolma stared at them, then said, "You gave me extra." Her ears burned for a second as she handed them back, and then her shoulders felt light. He nodded. "Thank you, beta."

Two days later she found a wallet under a park bench and took it straight to the gate guard. When Papa heard, he hugged her tight and she grinned. That night, in bed, she thought about it. The hug was lovely, but she would have returned it even if no one had ever told him.

qa.q: Where did Dolma find the hundred-rupee note?
qa.a: She found it near the water cooler.

qa.q: How did returning the note differ from handing back the coins and the wallet in what pushed Dolma and how she felt?
qa.a: With the note, friends pulled the other way and her stomach twisted before she chose. With the coins, nobody was watching, she felt awkward for a second and then light. With the wallet, Papa's hug felt lovely, but she knew she would have returned it anyway.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel about the chips plan, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Anjali seemed uneasy. Anjali said nothing during the plan and later murmured that spending it was not wanted either.

qa.q: What could Dolma do if a friend keeps pushing her to spend money that is not hers?
qa.a: She could repeat politely that she would rather not, and offer to walk the money to a teacher together.

grounding: One child meets a found note with friends urging her to spend it, a shopkeeper's extra change, and a returned wallet that earns a parent's hug.

passage:
Jagdish came home to find his sketchbook open on the floor, pages smudged with orange crayon. "Gautam!" he shouted so loudly the neighbours heard. His younger brother went pale and ran. Amma made Gautam say sorry and set a rule: ask first. Jagdish bought a padlocked tin for his best pencils, and that was that.

For two days the brothers did not speak. At dinner Amma asked Gautam about his spelling test for ages, and Jagdish stabbed his rice, sure she liked Gautam better. Later he said it out loud. "You never ask me anything." Amma blinked. "Tomorrow after homework, just you and me." On Saturday they walked to the lake together.

Meanwhile his little sister Jaya trailed him from room to room, poking at his marbles. "Bhaiya, what's this?" She adored him, and it was tiring. "These are mine, Jaya. But at five o'clock we can play ludo." She grinned and held him to it.

On Sunday Jagdish sat down next to Gautam with a packet of biscuits, snapped one, and slid half across. Gautam took it. "Sorry about the sketchbook." "Sorry I yelled," said Jagdish, and both of them crunched.

qa.q: What did Jagdish buy to keep his best pencils safe?
qa.a: He bought a padlocked tin for his best pencils.

qa.q: How did Jagdish's way of dealing with Jaya's constant following differ from how he dealt with the fight with Gautam?
qa.a: With Jaya he stayed kind and named a boundary, "These are mine", plus a time to play together. With Gautam he first shouted, then stayed silent for days, and only the small gesture of sharing a biscuit ended it.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when Amma kept asking Gautam about his spelling test?
qa.a: He felt overlooked and a little jealous. He stabbed his rice and was sure Amma liked Gautam better.

qa.q: Why did telling Amma out loud work better than staying quiet at dinner?
qa.a: Once he said it, Amma listened and planned time for just the two of them, so his feeling was met instead of growing at the table.

grounding: One older child handles a sibling using his sketchbook, feeling less loved, a little sister who follows him, and the silence after a fight.

passage:
Hemant lay curled up with a hot forehead, and Mummy sat by his bed, holding him close. He felt small and warm and safe. When she stood to fetch water, he grabbed her sleeve and whimpered, afraid and wobbly. "I will be back before your cartoon song ends, and I will come straight here," she said, and she was.

Next morning Papa took him to the clinic. At the sight of the needle, Hemant's heart thumped and tears rushed out. The doctor crouched down. "It will pinch for a moment and I am right here." It did pinch, and Hemant howled, but he held Papa's hand, and he was glad no one had pretended it would not hurt.

Back home, his sister Rukmini watched Hemant get soup, jelly and a soft blanket on the sofa. She kicked the table leg. "Why can't I be poorly as well?" she muttered, eyes wet. Mummy noticed, pulled her onto her lap, and said, "Hemant needs lots of sleep now, and you and I get story time." Rukmini leaned in, and after a while she went to fetch her brother a cushion.

qa.q: Who took Hemant to the clinic?
qa.a: Papa took him to the clinic.

qa.q: How was Mummy's answer to Hemant's clinging like the doctor's answer to his fear of the needle, and how was Rukmini's need different?
qa.a: Both told him plainly what would happen, that she would be back before the cartoon song ended and that it would pinch for a moment, and both stayed close. Rukmini needed something else: attention of her own, so Mummy gave her story time and explained Hemant needed sleep.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she muttered about being poorly as well?
qa.a: She felt jealous and left out. Her eyes were wet and she kicked the table leg.

qa.q: What might help Hemant at the next clinic visit?
qa.a: An adult telling him the truth again, that it will pinch briefly and they are right there, since he was glad nobody pretended it would not hurt.

grounding: One sick child clings to a parent, fears a needle and is cared for, while a sibling feels jealous of the attention in the same household.

The bid went to Northline, the bigger agency, and the office at Lavanya's small design firm went quiet. Mahima felt a hot, sour twist. She typed a sneering line about Northline's "cheap tricks" into the team chat, then deleted it, thinking how bad it would look. Instead she emailed the client and asked, politely, what had tipped the choice. The reply: faster turnaround and a named contact for every job.

Rukmini, the analyst, pulled up Northline's published case studies and spent a weekend comparing them with the firm's own. On Monday she brought a list: shorter proposals, a named contact, a price table clients could read. Lavanya nodded. "They are good at some things. Let's learn from them."

Lavanya herself lay awake a while, afraid of Northline's reach and its habit of chasing accounts. Next day she phoned her three best clients, offered each a review, and told the staff she would not cut corners or copy any aggressive tactics, only lean on what the firm did best: local knowledge and quick replies.

At a trade evening, Ashok from another agency talked about Northline for an hour, calling them thieves and worse. His own clients waited days for replies, and two of them quietly left by the end of the quarter.

qa.q: What did the client say tipped the choice toward Northline?
qa.a: Faster turnaround and a named contact for every job.

qa.q: How did Mahima's and Ashok's reactions to Northline's win lead to different results?
qa.a: Mahima deleted her sneer and asked the client what tipped the choice, so she learned about turnaround and a named contact. Ashok kept running Northline down, neglected his own clients, and lost two of them.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling that made her phone her best clients?
qa.a: She was afraid of Northline's reach and worried about losing accounts, so she reached out to protect the clients she had.

qa.q: What could Rukmini's list help the firm do next?
qa.a: It could help the firm shorten its proposals, name a contact for each job and show clear prices, improving without copying Northline's tactics.

grounding: The same lost bid is met with learning from the rival, obsessing about the rival, fear of the rival's reach, and envy that is held back and turned into questions.
